performers: Fyodor Chaliapin, bass; orchestra conducted by Albert Coates
intro: Chaliapin returned to The Prophet, Op. 49 No. 2, with Albert Coates in 1927. In Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral setting of Pushkin’s short poem, a single bass voice tells of an angel, a burning coal and a command from God.

sections.label: A · Andante, opening in the bass
sections.mNote: Measured vocal phrases set the opening of Pushkin’s poem.

sections.label: B · Voice over rippling accompaniment
sections.mNote: The bass describes the newly opened senses.

sections.label: C · Orchestral passage
sections.mNote: The accompaniment links the verses of the poem.

sections.label: D · Bass line moves forward
sections.mNote: The vocal line uses repeated notes.

sections.label: E · Tempo I returns
sections.mNote: The opening tempo returns at Tempo I.

sections.label: F · The prophet’s final charge, con forza
sections.mNote: Con forza e maestoso: forcefully and majestically.

cues.title: Opening, Andante
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov begins with firm chords and a quiet bass voice, marked Andante. Pushkin’s speaker is wandering in a dark desert. When a six-winged angel appears, his measured phrases open out and the accompaniment begins to ripple.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, Complete Collected Works, vol. 45 (Muzgiz, 1946; reprinted 1970), The Prophet, p. 91. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP20759-PMLP48251-Rimsky_Op49.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: London recording, 1927
cues.text: On 20 October 1927 Chaliapin recorded the song in London with Albert Coates. Six years earlier, on 10 October 1921, he had recorded it at Hayes with Percy Pitt. He sang it again in Russian, this time with a different conductor.
cues.evidence: Public Domain Project gives the London session and Coates: https://pool.publicdomainproject.org/index.php?title=Gramophone-db1103-2-022043. DAHR gives the 10 October 1921 Hayes session with Pitt: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/2000007905.

cues.title: Pushkin’s poem, lines 21–26
cues.text: In Pushkin’s poem, the angel cuts open the man’s chest, removes his trembling heart and puts a burning coal in its place. The man lies like a corpse in the desert. God speaks after this.
cues.evidence: Pushkin, The Prophet (1826), lines 21–26: https://rvb.ru/pt/pushkin/0420-ru.html. This note describes the poem’s narrative, independently of the sung words at this point.

cues.title: Final invocation
cues.text: The bass sings the final command, marked Con forza e maestoso, over continuous accompanying figures. In Pushkin’s text God sends the remade man across seas and lands to speak. The accompaniment continues after the voice stops.
cues.evidence: Complete Collected Works, vol. 45, p. 97: the final invocation is marked con forza e maestoso, above continuous accompanying figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP20759-PMLP48251-Rimsky_Op49.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Russian composer known for fairy-tale operas and his detailed knowledge of the orchestra; he became a professor before he had learned counterpoint.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, and his piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 on a voyage of nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, and took a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev, who replied with encouragement and requests for changes. Farther out, he saw the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue, flying fish and phosphorescence. After his return to Russia he took up music again, and Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
